scenario: AITA for not wanting to be friends with my group anymore? | So I just finished my freshman year in college, and I found myself a pretty good friend group. I’ve always been really shy so the fact that I‘m part of a group means a lot to me. However, I’m the only one (in a group of 8) that is not in our school’s Honors College. Many people, including them, have assured me that this doesn’t mean they’re smarter than me or harder working than me, and I’ve accepted that. However, Honors College people all have some required courses to take that are just for them, so they all have classes together without me. And sometimes when we hang out, everyone talks about their classes and I feel completely left out. In addition, I found out that next year, they’re all living in the Honors College dorm building together. I can’t live there since I’m not in Honors College and I already feel left out enough. Now that they’ll all live together, it’s even more likely they’ll end up hanging out without me just because they’re all living together and just happen to run into each other and how can I blame them for that?? I have tried to talk to a couple of them about it and one in particular said that I have no right to make them feel bad for being happy that they can live together but I feel like if they had an ounce of empathy, they’d realize that 7 people of an 8 person group living together is rather unfair. I don’t want to have to start over and find new friends but I also feel like I deserve friends who will try to include me. AITA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for me to feel this way about my friends. Let me start by understanding the situation better. I just finished my freshman year in college, and I've managed to find a pretty good friend group. Considering I've always been really shy, being part of a group means a lot to me. But here's the thing: I'm the only one in a group of eight who isn't in our school's Honors College. Now, people, including my friends, have told me that this doesn't mean they're smarter or harder working than me, and I've tried to accept that. However, the Honors College students have some required courses that are just for them, so they all have classes together without me. That's already a bit isolating because when we hang out, everyone talks about their classes, and I feel completely left out. To make things worse, I found out that next year, they're all living in the Honors College dorm building together. I can't live there since I'm not in the Honors College, and I already feel left out enough. Now that they'll all live together, it's even more likely they'll end up hanging out without me just because they're all living together and happen to run into each other. I can't blame them for that, can I? I've tried talking to a couple of them about it, and one person in particular said that I have no right to make them feel bad for being happy that they can live together. But I feel like if they had an ounce of empathy, they'd realize that seven people of an eight-person group living together is rather unfair. I don't want to have to start over and find new friends, but I also feel like I deserve friends who will try to include me. So, is it AITA (Ask a Internet Therapist/Advisor) for me to feel this way? Am I overreacting, or is this a valid concern? I need to figure out whether my feelings are justified or if I'm being too sensitive. First, I need to understand what AITA means. From what I gather, it's about whether the situation is something that others would consider reasonable or not. So, is it reasonable for me to feel upset about being excluded because my friends are all living together in a dorm that I can't access? I think it's important to consider the dynamics of the group. I'm the only one not in the Honors College, and that seems to be creating a divide. The fact that they have classes together without me already makes me feel left out, and now the living situation is exacerbating that feeling. On one hand, it's natural for people to want to live with their friends, especially if they're already close. On the other hand, it's understandable that I feel excluded and worried about losing my friend group. I also need to think about how I've tried to communicate my feelings. I talked to a couple of them, and one person responded by saying I shouldn't make them feel bad for being happy. That response might have made me feel like my concerns aren't being validated, which could be contributing to my frustration. Is it fair to expect my friends to make an effort to include me even though they're living together? Or is it reasonable for them to prioritize their own happiness and convenience? I guess it's a balance between their needs and mine. I also wonder if there's a way to maintain the friendship without feeling excluded. Maybe we can find other ways to hang out or make plans that include me even if they're living together. It might require some effort from both sides, but I don't know if that's realistic. Another thing to consider is whether I'm projecting my insecurities onto the situation. Being shy and finding a friend group is a big deal, so it's natural to feel anxious about losing that. But is that anxiety making me overreact to the situation? I also need to think about whether I'm being too idealistic about friendships. Friendships can change, and people's circumstances can lead to different dynamics. It's possible that the friendship group will naturally evolve, and that's okay. But does that mean I have to accept feeling excluded, or can I work to maintain the friendship in a different way? I also wonder if there's a way to approach the situation differently. Maybe instead of focusing on the exclusion, I can focus on finding ways to stay connected despite the living situation. Or perhaps I can explore other friend groups or activities that can help me feel included and valued. In the end, I think it's important to validate my feelings. Feeling excluded and worried about losing friends is a valid concern, especially when you've worked hard to build those relationships. However, I also need to consider the practical aspects of the situation and whether there's a way to navigate it in a way that respects both my needs and my friends' needs. Maybe the answer isn't as simple as right or wrong, but rather about finding a balance and understanding that friendships can change and evolve over time. It's okay to feel upset, but it's also important to approach the situation with empathy and understanding for both myself and my friends.
